claim.pdf_says: 3. When the sending operand is described as alphanumeric or national, the sending operand is treated as if it were an unsigned integer of category numeric with the following characteristics: [indented beneath it] a. If the sending operand is a data item, ... b. If the sending operand is a figurative constant, ... c. If the sending operand is an alphanumeric or national literal, ...
claim.markdown_says:
3\. When the sending operand is described as alphanumeric or national, ...

   a. If the sending operand is a data item, ...

   b. If the sending operand is a figurative constant, ...

   c. If the sending operand is an alphanumeric or national literal, ...

   c) When a receiving item is described as alphabetic, ...
claim.why_it_matters: In MOVE general rule 4b the printed page nests items a.-c. under item 3. (they are the characteristics of the alphanumeric/national sending operand); the markdown puts a.-c. at the same indentation as 1.-3. and as the parent-level c) and d), so the sub-items are detached from item 3 and read as siblings of it.

verdict.reasoning: The printed page (p.480 of ISO/IEC 1989:2002, PDF page 502) does indent a.-c. one level under item 3., and items 1.-3. one level under rule b), and the markdown flattens every list to the same 3-space indent. But all text is present and correctly quoted and ordered; the only difference is indentation. The nesting stays unambiguous in the markdown: item 3 ends with 'with the following characteristics:' and is followed directly by items labelled with a distinct style (a./b./c., lowercase letter with period), which differs from both the numeric siblings (1./2./3.) and the parent-level labels (c)/d) with a parenthesis). No reader can take a.-c. as siblings of 3. or of c)/d). This is list-indentation formatting that does not change meaning, so per the reject criteria it is not a genuine content discrepancy.
